title: The Apology
author: Plato
length: One defense speech in three parts
openingText: I don't know what impression my accusers have made on you, Athenians, but they almost made me forget who I was, they spoke so persuasively. Yet they have hardly said a word of truth.
about:
Plato presents Socrates defending himself before an Athenian court. The accusations are that he corrupts the young and does not acknowledge the city's gods. Here, an apology means a defense, not an expression of regret. Socrates answers both the formal charges and the older rumors that, he says, have shaped the jurors' view of him since childhood.

The speech has three parts. Socrates first explains his questioning of politicians, poets and craftsmen, then questions his accuser Meletus. After the guilty verdict, he discusses the penalty he deserves. Finally, after the death sentence, he addresses both those who condemned him and those who would have acquitted him.

His defense turns on a distinction between knowing and merely believing that one knows. That distinction also shapes his attitude to death: he does not claim to know whether it is bad. He insists that wrongdoing is bad and refuses to abandon his questions to avoid a danger he does not understand. The speech invites us to test that argument, as well as the effect of his manner on the people judging him.

whyItMatters.title: Knowing the limits of knowledge
whyItMatters.body: Socrates visits people with reputations for wisdom and finds that their confidence extends beyond what they know. Skilled craftsmen really do possess knowledge, but that does not make them experts in everything. His account asks how a person can recognize the boundary between expertise and assumption.

whyItMatters.title: Justice under pressure
whyItMatters.body: Socrates recalls refusing an unlawful collective trial under the democracy and refusing an order to fetch a man for execution under the Thirty. He presents these actions as evidence that fear of death will not make him do what he considers wrong. Readers can compare that claim with his conduct in the trial itself.

whyItMatters.title: The city's troublesome critic
whyItMatters.body: Socrates compares Athens to a large, sluggish horse and himself to a gadfly that keeps it awake. He asks whether citizens benefit from uncomfortable questioning even when they dislike the questioner. His opponents' response, and his own refusal to stop, give that question immediate consequences.

angleCards.title: Follow the questions
angleCards.text: Track how Socrates turns Meletus' answers into a challenge to the accusation. Where does the argument persuade you, and where might you resist it?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Socrates' reasoning and test whether his questions establish what he claims.

angleCards.title: Consider the refusal to plead
angleCards.text: Socrates will not bring his children before the court to ask for pity. Examine his reasons and the distinction he draws between persuasion and a favor.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Socrates' refusal to plead for pity and test his account of a judge's duty.

angleCards.title: Ask what examination requires
angleCards.text: Watch what Socrates asks people to care about and what he means by examining a life.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the examined life and consider what practicing it would involve.

angleCards.title: Compare the two accounts of death
angleCards.text: Socrates considers unconsciousness and a journey to another world. Notice which claims are possibilities and which he treats as certainties.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Socrates' argument about death without turning his hopes into claims of knowledge.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: An Athenian who says he is over seventy and appearing before a court for the first time. He defends his practice of questioning others and refuses to promise that he will stop.

cast.name: Meletus
cast.description: Socrates questions him about who improves the young and whether the indictment accuses Socrates of believing in no gods or in different divine beings.

cast.name: Anytus and Lycon
cast.description: Socrates says Anytus speaks for craftsmen and politicians, while Lycon speaks for orators. He links all three accusers to the resentment his questioning has aroused.

cast.name: The Athenian jurors
cast.description: They vote first on guilt and then on the penalty. Socrates says that thirty votes changing sides would have acquitted him; that is not the same as a thirty-vote winning margin.

cast.name: Chaerephon
cast.description: He asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer, Socrates says, prompted him to investigate what the god could mean.

cast.name: Crito, Critobulus, Plato and Apollodorus
cast.description: During the penalty discussion, Socrates names these friends as guarantors for a proposed fine of thirty minae.
